findings.text: Within the first two sentences a newcomer can say what Athena is. The page also explains what sets it apart: a second model checks the work, and the cost of each step is recorded.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page says why it exists: it is a demonstration. It also explains early that a "study" is a reading of another project fixed at one commit. That keeps the newcomer from wondering why Athena's own site is about a different tool.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: Apart from the three-paragraph header and Next steps, everything on Athena's own site is about firstmate. A newcomer who wants to judge Athena learns its features from one sentence and has to infer its value from the shape of a long, dense example.
findings.source: Page title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and the sections that follow (States, Counters, Transitions t1–t11, Claims c1–c44)

findings.text: The page gives the next step at the top and links to it, so the newcomer doesn't have to scroll through the whole study to find out how to act.
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" linking to #next-steps

findings.text: The install step assumes the reader already has a checkout. There is no clone command, no list of prerequisites (Rust toolchain, model access or API keys), and no note on which repository the example `athena ask` runs against. A newcomer may get stuck between the link and the first command.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: Some terms are left undefined or defined only in terms of themselves. "Wake", "captain call", "endpoint" and "heartbeat" are never explained, so a stranger can't follow those parts of the firstmate walkthrough.
findings.source: Glossary: "stale wake — A wake after which the agent inspects a worker that may have stopped, looped or gone quiet."; Start here: "If the backlog item is still an open captain call, teardown reopens it"

findings.text: The firstmate part is well organized for a first-time reader. It gives a one-sentence summary, defines key words before using them, and walks one task in order before the detailed cards.
findings.source: Start here: "Words used first" list and "One piece of work, start to finish"

findings.text: Every statement can be traced to a claim and then to linked lines at a pinned commit, and the page tells the reader how to check one. This makes Athena's main promise concrete and lets the reader verify it.
findings.source: Header lede: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it"; Next steps: "Check a statement: follow a bracketed claim id to the claim, then its source link"

findings.text: The page is open about the fact that nothing was run, only read. That builds trust, but it also means the demonstration doesn't show Athena's headline ability: turning a request into a checked change.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read"
